questions.prompt: What does a color image's shape (height, width, channels) with channels=3 represent?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The three RGB color channels — Red, Green, and Blue — each contributing to every pixel's final color

A standard color image stores three separate grids of values (one per Red, Green, Blue channel), all the same height and width — combining the three values at each position produces that pixel's full color.
keyPoints: A standard color image stores three separate grids of values (one per Red, Green, Blue channel), all the same height and width — combining the three values at each position produces that pixel's full color.

questions.prompt: Why might a horizontal flip be a safe augmentation for a photo of a cat, but not for a photo of text?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A flipped cat photo still clearly shows a cat, but flipped text becomes unreadable and no longer represents valid text for an OCR task

Whether an augmentation is appropriate depends on whether it preserves the label's correctness for the specific task — a flipped cat is still recognizably a cat, but flipped text is no longer valid, readable text, making that augmentation inappropriate for an OCR task.
keyPoints: Whether an augmentation is appropriate depends on whether it preserves the label's correctness for the specific task — a flipped cat is still recognizably a cat, but flipped text is no longer valid, readable text, making that augmentation inappropriate for an OCR task.

questions.prompt: What does 'backbone' refer to in a vision model?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The core feature-extracting part of the model, which can be reused across different tasks by swapping the final task-specific layers

The backbone is the shared feature-extraction portion of a vision model (typically the convolutional layers) — the same backbone can support classification, detection, or segmentation by changing only the final task-specific layers, connecting directly to transfer learning.
keyPoints: The backbone is the shared feature-extraction portion of a vision model (typically the convolutional layers) — the same backbone can support classification, detection, or segmentation by changing only the final task-specific layers, connecting directly to transfer learning.

questions.prompt: What does Intersection over Union (IoU) measure?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: How well a predicted bounding box overlaps with the true (ground truth) bounding box

IoU is computed as the overlapping area between two boxes divided by their combined (union) area, giving a standard way to measure how accurately a predicted box's location matches the true box.
keyPoints: IoU is computed as the overlapping area between two boxes divided by their combined (union) area, giving a standard way to measure how accurately a predicted box's location matches the true box.

questions.prompt: What does semantic segmentation predict for an image?
questions.referenceAnswer: Unlike classification (one label per image) or detection (a box per object), semantic segmentation produces a full-resolution output where every pixel is individually labeled with its category.
keyPoints: Unlike classification (one label per image) or detection (a box per object), semantic segmentation produces a full-resolution output where every pixel is individually labeled with its category.

choices.text: A single label for the whole image
A bounding box around each object
A class label for every individual pixel in the image
A text caption describing the image

questions.prompt: What are the two main stages of a typical OCR pipeline?
questions.referenceAnswer: OCR typically works in two stages: first detecting where text regions exist in the image (similar to object detection, but for text), and then recognizing the actual characters within each detected region.
keyPoints: OCR typically works in two stages: first detecting where text regions exist in the image (similar to object detection, but for text), and then recognizing the actual characters within each detected region.

choices.text: Image classification and image compression
Text detection (finding where text is located) and text recognition (reading what the text says)
Data augmentation and model training only
Color correction and noise removal only

questions.prompt: Why might a model trained mostly on well-lit daytime photos struggle with nighttime images?
questions.referenceAnswer: This mirrors the data science course's core principle — a model can only learn to handle conditions actually represented in its training data, so if nighttime or unusual lighting wasn't well represented, the model has no learned basis for handling those conditions well.
keyPoints: This mirrors the data science course's core principle — a model can only learn to handle conditions actually represented in its training data, so if nighttime or unusual lighting wasn't well represented, the model has no learned basis for handling those conditions well.

Vision models are technically incapable of processing dark images
Lighting conditions have no actual effect on model performance

questions.prompt: Why might a project with a limited, small task-specific dataset favor a CNN over a ViT?
questions.referenceAnswer: Since ViTs must learn useful spatial patterns from data alone (lacking a CNN's built-in convolutional bias), they generally need more training examples to perform comparably well — making a pretrained CNN a more practical, reliable choice when task-specific data is limited.
keyPoints: Since ViTs must learn useful spatial patterns from data alone (lacking a CNN's built-in convolutional bias), they generally need more training examples to perform comparably well — making a pretrained CNN a more practical, reliable choice when task-specific data is limited.

questions.prompt: An image classifier fails when deployed to a different camera. What would you inspect first, and why?

keyPoints: Separate input-pipeline errors from domain shift.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.
